lnk-dpm.title: The Palace Museum · Digital Cultural Relics
lnk-dpm.note: The copyright notice is unambiguous: no commercial use, no systematic extraction, no robotic harvesting, and no building of a similar database. So Chenhua keeps only an index card and a link — no image fetched, none cached. The red line is not an obstacle; it is what lets an archive like this last.

1843-daguerreotype.title: A man photographed himself into the studio
1843-daguerreotype.note: In 1839 Daguerre announced the daguerreotype. Within a few years someone had turned the lens on himself. Before that, leaving a likeness of “I am here” took a brush and someone else's hand; after, light could do it alone. What Chenhua collects begins at this moment — including this slightly nervous self-portrait.

1840s-priest.title: A priest in daguerreotype
1840s-priest.note: The exposure took tens of seconds. He had to quiet his breath and fix his gaze on a point that did not exist. Portraits of that era carry a trace of held breath. No battle, no treaty — just a man deciding to spend money to keep himself. History's thickest layer has always been made of moments like this, with no names.

lnk-bm.title: The British Museum · Collection images
lnk-bm.note: Open, but explicitly non-commercial. The moment a site runs ads, takes sponsorship or funnels traffic, this material has to come down wholesale. So it sits apart in a text-only link card, governed by the usage-mode switch — no image hidden, no line crossed.

1852-bridge.title: The bridge at Paralda
1852-bridge.note: A salt print from a waxed-paper negative, of a bridge no one remembers. The photographer had to coat, expose and develop on site, and came away with only a few plates, so every shutter release began with a question: is it worth it? He thought it was. The street corner you photograph today may be looked at this carefully in a hundred years.

1860-taku.title: The Taku Forts: the corner the French stormed
1860-taku.note: An albumen print, 1860. The catalog title says it plainly: “the angle of the Taku Forts through which the French forces entered” — even the direction of the view becomes testimony. These images from the Second Opium War are among the earliest photographic records of China; most of the negatives ended up abroad, and have to be brought back one by one.

1863-soldier.title: The soldier lying down
1863-soldier.note: A portrait from the American Civil War, and the man is lying down. No charge, no flag, only a pose. Great events are never made only of generals and dates; in the end they land on one specific person — here, not even his name survives.

1860s-tintype.title: Andy Wilson's tintype
1860s-tintype.note: Tintypes were cheap, fast and hardy — the portrait ordinary people could afford. The catalog calls him a “contraband,” a servant in the Civil War's vocabulary. The name survives; a life is reduced to this small sheet of iron. This is the kind of image Chenhua most wants to keep: someone written down in passing by the great sweep of history.

1871-paris-barricade.title: The barricade on Rue de Castiglione
1871-paris-barricade.note: Paris Commune, 1871, Rue de Castiglione, a barricade built of paving stones. No charge in the photograph, only stacked stone and a few men standing. The longest stretch of an uprising is waiting. The street name survives; the men who stacked the stones do not.

1875-market.title: Market day outside the city wall
1875-market.note: Outside the city wall, stalls set out, someone choosing goods, someone just standing and talking. Nothing happened that day, and precisely for that it was painted. Only with such scenes on the same axis as wars and moon landings does the human world become whole: most days have no title.

1888-eiffel-construction.title: When the tower was half built
1888-eiffel-construction.note: In 1888 Louis-Émile Durandelle photographed the Eiffel Tower under construction. The steel was still a skeleton assembled floor by floor; Paris went about its life at its feet. Later it became the city's signature, but here it looks more like an unfinished building site.

commons-1900-beijing.title: Beijing in 1900
commons-1900-beijing.note: Beijing in 1900: city walls, street corners and passers-by all caught on the same negative. China was being photographed earlier than people usually assume; most of these images are scattered in collections abroad, like finding your own old letters in someone else's drawer. Chenhua wants to bring them back, one by one.

1900-women.title: Two women who left no names
1900-women.note: A cabinet card, ca. 1900. Two women dressed carefully and seated side by side, clearly prepared for the day. The catalog title says only “two unidentified women.” “Unidentified” is not a defect; it is how most people remain in history: seen, not remembered.

1900-mailcar.title: Boston's mail streetcar
1900-mailcar.note: Ca. 1900, a streetcar in Boston that sorted mail on board. Letters were postmarked and sorted into slots as the car ran along the tracks — how a city actually works is often more honest than any manifesto. We keep it because the earliest shape of “modern life” usually hides in infrastructure like this.

lnk-loc.title: Library of Congress · Unassessed images
lnk-loc.note: “No known restrictions” sounds like a pass, but it only means the library found no restrictions. Not finding one is not the same as none existing. Records like this wait in the verification pool until first publication and rights status are checked one by one.

1908-boy.title: The boy at the loom
1908-boy.note: A cotton mill in Indiana, around 1908. He stands at the loom, just tall enough to reach the machine. The four characters “Industrial Revolution” land on one person at exactly this height. Chenhua puts this on the same timeline as the Moon landing not to elevate it, but to keep the scale from flipping.

commons-1912-titanic.title: Titanic leaving Southampton
commons-1912-titanic.note: 10 April 1912, departure. No iceberg, no band, just a ship leaving the dock as if nothing were about to happen. The story told for a century is all compressed into this departure photograph where nothing happens — the most understated foreshadowing an image can offer.

1915-suffrage.title: A women's suffrage postcard
1915-suffrage.note: 1915: a postcard meant to be sent, pinned to a desk corner, pushed into a drawer. The movement did not happen only in parliament; it seeped into daily life through paper like this, a penny a sheet. Great events have their own popular circulation history, and it rarely looks like a monument.

1918-influenza-ward.title: 1918: an influenza ward
1918-influenza-ward.note: New Orleans naval hospital, 1918. An influenza patient being treated. The pandemic was later reduced to a number in the millions, but the lens leaves only a bed, a person leaning over, and a curtain someone hung. History's heaviest part often hides in rooms like this, with no sound.

1918-redcross-station.title: A demonstration at a Red Cross first-aid station
1918-redcross-station.note: 1918, at a Red Cross first-aid station, a group demonstrates ambulance work. No patients, no chaos, only neat ranks and carefully laid-out equipment — what the pandemic rehearsed most was “being ready.”

commons-1930-shanghai.title: Nanjing Road in the 1930s
commons-1930-shanghai.note: Signs, trams, pedestrians: a street that writes its own decade plainly enough to need no date. The word “era” always lands on one specific street — who walks there, what the shops sell, what typeface the signs use. This unsigned street view is closer to its time than many chronicles.

commons-1936-migrant.title: Migrant Mother
commons-1936-migrant.note: March 1936, Dorothea Lange pressed the shutter at a pea-picking camp in California. The macro numbers of the Depression become one face and several children turning away. Later it became the cover of an entire era — but on the day, no one knew.

commons-1944-dday.title: “Into the Jaws of Death”
commons-1944-dday.note: 6 June 1944, Omaha Beach. The archive number is 23-0455M; the title is “Into the Jaws of Death.” Sometimes a great event leaves only a number, a group of backs facing the camera, and a metaphor even the official record could not resist.

1945-vmail.title: A V-Mail letter
1945-vmail.note: 13 February 1945. To save shipping space, letters home were microfilmed, flown across the ocean, and enlarged again on arrival. Half of war is the front; the other half is the people waiting for a reply. This thin sheet touches both. We collect the letter, not the battle.

commons-1945-hiroshima.title: Hiroshima, after the bomb
commons-1945-hiroshima.note: An aerial photograph from August 1945. Almost no detail survives, only a city erased flat. Some images should be neither beautified nor omitted. Chenhua keeps the record without judging, but keeps its weight — and the few seconds that make you stop.

commons-1945-iwojima.title: The flag on Iwo Jima
commons-1945-iwojima.note: 23 February 1945, Joe Rosenthal. The moment was later printed on stamps, cast in bronze, reproduced without end. How a photograph becomes memory, and how memory then covers the photograph, is itself a history worth archiving.

1968-earthrise-first.title: Seeing Earthrise for the first time
1968-earthrise-first.note: December 1968. Apollo 8 swung behind the Moon and came back around; Earth suddenly rose above the lunar horizon. Archive number AS08-13-2329. Humans had photographed Earth countless times, but never as “the place we live” rising as a celestial body. Nearly every later claim about the whole begins with this frame.

commons-1969-bootprint.title: One footprint
commons-1969-bootprint.note: To test whether the lunar soil would hold, Aldrin pressed down a boot print and took a photograph. No wind, no rain; it will probably stay for a long time. The quietest evidence left by something as large as the Moon landing is this — great and small events belong on the same axis.

1969-saturn.title: Saturn V
1969-saturn.note: The rocket that put people on the Moon. Historical events often need an object to testify: a document, an artefact, a photograph. This frame has no human face, only a machine that was built — perhaps the most honest self-portrait of its era.

1969-plaque.title: The plaque left on the Moon
1969-plaque.note: 20 July 1969. A metal plaque was left on the lunar surface: “We came in peace for all mankind.” For the first time, humans placed a sentence addressed to everyone outside the Earth. The date is precise to the day; the subject is “we” — the standard shape of a great event.

commons-1969-aldrin.title: The photographer reflected in the visor
commons-1969-aldrin.note: 20 July 1969. Aldrin stands on the Moon; in his gold visor, Armstrong is reflected holding the camera. Humanity's farthest journey still comes down to two people: one photographed, one photographing. Every grand narrative breaks down into this division of labour.

1981-sts1.title: STS-1 lifts off
1981-sts1.note: NASA's original caption begins, “After six years of silence.” On 12 April 1981 the shuttle left the launch pad for the first time. Even the official archive could not resist an emotional opening — a measure of how long the wait had been.

commons-1989-berlin.title: Juggling on the Berlin Wall
commons-1989-berlin.note: November 1989. The Wall had not fallen yet, and someone was already up on it, juggling. The most moving evidence of a turning point is often not the official photograph but someone's improvisation: a structure built to divide suddenly became a stage.

2012-earth.title: Looking down from the International Space Station
2012-earth.note: 2012, a frame looking down from low Earth orbit. No borders, no place names, only cloud and sea. The contemporary image that most resembles “a common human history” usually comes from the farthest place from humans — far enough that no one is visible, and yet it is all about people.

2022-artemis.title: Artemis I flight readiness review
2022-artemis.note: August 2022, a flight readiness review in session. History does not happen only at ignition; it forms slowly in countless meeting-room photographs: someone bent over papers, someone facing a screen. We collect these “not yet” images too.

2026-earthset.title: Earthset from Orion
2026-earthset.note: April 2026. As the Orion spacecraft skimmed past the lunar limb, Earth was setting. NASA's caption notes that it echoes the famous “Earthrise.” More than half a century later, the equipment has changed, a generation has changed, and the direction of the gaze has not.
